q: An inertial frame is a frame of reference that has no acceleration. (2024)
e: An inertial frame is defined as a reference frame that is not accelerating.

q: The term “radioactivity” is used to describe the rate at which a radioactive sample undergoes decay. (2024)
e: The rate at which a sample decays is called activity, while radioactivity refers to the process of spontaneous nuclear decay.

q: Gamma rays can be deflected by electric and magnetic fields. (2024)
e: Gamma rays consist of uncharged photons, so they are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.

q: A nuclear reaction is a process in which a beta radiation penetrates into a nucleus and changes its configuration. (2024)
e: A nuclear reaction occurs when atomic nuclei or subatomic particles collide to produce new nuclei.

q: In β⁻ decay, the atomic number of daughter nucleus increases by one. (2024)
e: In beta-minus decay, a neutron transforms into a proton, increasing the atomic number by 1.

q: Activity of a radioactive sample decreases with time. (2024)
e: As unstable nuclei decay over time, fewer remain, causing the sample's activity to decrease.

q: Relativistic effect usually becomes negligible when speed of the system becomes comparable to the speed of light. (2024)
e: Relativistic effects become significant, not negligible, as speeds approach the speed of light.

q: The wave nature of electrons is used instead of light in electron microscope. (2025)
e: Electron microscopes exploit the short de Broglie wavelength of electrons to achieve high resolution.

q: All elements in nature are not radioactive. (2025)
e: Most naturally occurring elements and isotopes are stable rather than radioactive.

q: Alpha particles consist of two protons and neutrons making them identical to a helium nucleus. (2025)
e: An alpha particle contains two protons and two neutrons, identical to a helium-4 nucleus.

q: An inertial frame is a frame of reference that has no acceleration. (2025)
e: Inertial frames move at constant velocity with zero acceleration.

q: Beta particles are high-energy electrons or positrons emitted during radioactive decay. (2025)
e: Beta decay emits high-speed electrons (beta-minus) or positrons (beta-plus).

q: Positron is also called the antiparticle of proton. (2025)
e: A positron is the antiparticle of an electron, not a proton.

q: Gamma rays have no charge. (2025)
e: Gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic waves and carry zero electric charge.

q: In β⁻ decay, the atomic number of daughter nucleus increases by one. (2025)
e: Beta-minus decay converts a neutron into a proton, raising the atomic number by one.

q: Alpha rays can be deflected by electric and magnetic fields. (2025)
e: Alpha rays consist of positively charged particles (+2e), so electric and magnetic fields deflect them.

q: Shielding is a protective barrier, usually a dense material. (2025)
e: Dense materials such as lead or concrete are used as shielding to absorb radiation.

q: Beta rays are less penetrating than alpha rays. (2025)
e: Beta rays have greater penetrating power than alpha rays because of their smaller mass and lower ionisation density.

q: Neutrons released from a fission reaction are slow neutrons. (2026)
e: Nuclear fission directly releases fast (high-energy) neutrons.

q: Gamma rays can be stopped by a thick sheet of paper. (2026)
e: A thick sheet of paper stops alpha particles; gamma rays require thick lead or concrete to attenuate.

q: The Michelson Morley experiment provide evidence for the existence of the ether. (2026)
e: The Michelson-Morley experiment yielded a null result, disproving the presence of a luminiferous ether.
